items.claim: Because a bypassed upload check can land a file whose contents the server then executes, an upload bypass finding is only complete once the stored file is shown executing on the server.
items.body:
Because a bypassed upload check can land a file whose contents the server then executes, an upload bypass finding is only complete once the stored file is shown executing on the server.

HackTricks reference: file upload (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/file-upload-bypass/file_upload.md)
items.disproof: The accepted file is renamed, stored outside any executable path and served back as inert content with no execution on the server.

sources.quote: If a web application has this type of vulnerability, an aggressor can upload a file with malicious code in it that can be executed on the server.
This is especially true for web-server extensions such as .asp and .php because these file types are often treated as automatically executable
Whilst the file extension cannot be controlled (due to the timestamp being appended), the attacker can write files to arbitrary folders, with a partly controlled file name.

items.claim: End-user upload capability is a high-value target on its own, because a single accepted file can host a phishing page on the site's own origin or expose internal web server data.
items.body:
End-user upload capability is a high-value target on its own, because a single accepted file can host a phishing page on the site's own origin or expose internal web server data.

HackTricks reference: file upload (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/file-upload-bypass/file_upload.md)
items.disproof: Uploads are quarantined in a non-public, non-executable location and no uploaded content is served from the site's origin or reveals server-side data.

sources.quote:
An assailant may most likely put a phishing page into the site or mutilate it to uncover internal data of the web server to other people.
* Allowing file uploads by end-users, especially if done without a full understanding of the risks associated with it, is akin to opening the floodgates for server compromise.
This is especially true for web-server extensions such as .asp and .php because these file types are often treated as automatically executable
Whilst the file extension cannot be controlled (due to the timestamp being appended), the attacker can write files to arbitrary folders, with a partly controlled file name.
